thesis: This episode argues that early-stage investing focuses on identifying foundational technologies with significant future potential, such as Ethereum's trustless nature and decentralized applications, rather than just current market prices. The speaker highlights that successful early investments are characterized by growing real-world usage and adoption by credible companies, even when prices are low or volatile.

claims.claim: The speaker is a strong bull on Ethereum, citing its ability to enable trustless transactions and computations as a foundational technology with significant future potential.
claims.quote: And so, and I'm a, I should point out, I'm a strong bull on Ethereum, but my point in sharing this is actually that if the innovators themselves cannot exactly quantify the future value, how can investors, you know, even do that, right?

claims.claim: The speaker believes Ethereum's ability to be a decentralized trustless form of interaction is its strongest aspect and the reason for being bullish on it.
claims.quote: But that's actually specifically what personally I'm most excited about about Ethereum is its ability to truly be a decentralized trustless form of interaction, which has applications to all sorts of things.

claims.claim: The speaker is bullish on Ethereum because of its novel, precedent-free nature and early signs of adoption by credible companies like DocuSign.
claims.quote: And I think that's amazing. So that's why I'm bullish on it. It's just clearly, and then when you look at, I actually have a newspaper clipping from the financial times from like six months ago when the recent crypto winter hit, where it said something like the, I'm going to ruin the title here, but it's something like questions over the utility of Ethereum rise as price plummets.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that Coinbase's usage was growing week over week regardless of price, indicating real utility and making it a strong example of a successful early investment.
claims.quote: And then when you look within the current space, we're in like a crypto winter. It's a pretty bad one. And yet projects that have been around forever, like, Gallum, the decentralized compute network, usage has 5x in last year, despite the drop in price, like, 90%, or whatever, it has been.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions using Uber five times in the last two days and finds it indispensable, comparing its success to Coinbase's.
claims.quote: In the same way that Uber is amazing, because I've used it five times in the last two days, and it's indispensable to me.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Coinbase is a hugely successful business built around the primary interaction with cryptocurrencies, serving as a gateway for buying and selling.
claims.quote: Coinbase, obviously, has been a hugely successful business, largely because people use it like crazy. In the same way that Uber is amazing, because I've used it five times in the last two days, and it's indispensable to me. Coinbase is a company built around what to this point has been the primary interaction with cryptocurrencies, which is to buy and sell them.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions the Maker DAO project as an example of a decentralized stable coin with DAI, describing it as an entire financial institution that is completely self-running and decentralized.
claims.quote: And I think these projects have subsequently got some traction. And so it's somewhat becoming more mainstream, but like the Maker Dow project. sort of the idea of a decentralized stable coin with DAI die, their first major token to get adoption, which, and they'll be introducing multi-collateral die soon.

claims.claim: The speaker points to DocuSign announcing an integration with the Ethereum blockchain for e-signing as a ledger as evidence of real adoption by credible companies.
claims.quote: You see real adoption from blockchain from real companies, you know, like DocuSign, I believe, announced an integration with the Ethereum blockchain for e-signing as a ledger for that.

claims.claim: The speaker expresses hope and confidence that Ethereum will be big due to the theoretical utility of the technology and early signs of adoption.
claims.quote: So that's really the uniqueness of the technology. the theoretical utility of it and the early signs that it's actually being adopted by credible people and the early use cases that people are actually using these things for gives me a lot of hope and confidence in that somehow, in some way, this is going to be big.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Vitalik, creator of Ethereum, sold 25% of his stake of Ethereum at $10 per ether in early 2016 due to needing diversification.
claims.quote: And you see that even, like, today in the blockchain space of Vitalik, creator of Ethereum, along with the community of developers behind Ethereum, early on in 2016, sold 25% of his stake of Ethereum at $10 per, you know, ether.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that if Vitalik had waited 18 months after selling his Ethereum stake, it would have been 30 times more valuable.
claims.quote: But if he had just waited 18 months, it would have been 30 times more of value.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Gallium, a decentralized compute network, noting that its usage has increased 5x in the last year despite a significant drop in price.
claims.quote: And yet projects that have been around forever, like, Gallum, the decentralized compute network, usage has 5x in last year, despite the drop in price, like, 90%, or whatever, it has been.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that in 2012, the price of Bitcoin was like $6 and most people did not know what Bitcoin was.
claims.quote: And we'll start with Coinbase, but we'll go to like some other like less well-known examples as well. But like, coin was just such an epic one in the sense that in 2012, you know, the price of Bitcoin was like $6. And most people did not know what Bitcoin was, had never even heard of it.
